Throughout human history, philosophy has continued to develop, constantly expanding the range of its questions and answers.

But it is philosophy in the strict sense only when it asks its own questions and answers them by its own means: by discursive or logical means, without looking for either questions or answers in some supposedly nonhuman or divine “revelation.”

At a certain point in its historical development, philosophy realized that the “wisdom” it had sought from the beginning—the human ability to answer every concrete question concerning human beings themselves, their lives, and their actions—was nothing other than perfect knowledge or omniscience: the ability to answer every question that could possibly be asked.
Even after reaching this conclusion, philosophy continued to assume two things.
First, this omniscience must be reached by purely human and discursive means.
Second, it must be sought within humanity itself, not outside humanity and not in God.
Once the philosopher understood that the search for “wisdom” was really a search for omniscience, he was not frightened by the conclusion.
He continued to seek what had for centuries been attributed to God alone.
To aim openly and consciously at omniscience may be one of the clearest expressions of the freedom, boldness, and pride of human thought.
But this ambition should not be dismissed as pathological arrogance or megalomania.

Philosophy may assume, on the one hand, that some particular individual will in fact be the first person to reach perfect knowledge. But it also knows, on the other hand, that this knowledge will not belong to that individual alone.
The philosopher who first reaches “wisdom” is only the final link in a long chain of philosophical attempts to reach omniscience.
The achievement will therefore belong not only to that philosopher personally, but also to philosophy as a whole.

And since, as we will see again, the historical development of philosophy is nothing other than the ideal reflection—the “ideological superstructure”—of real historical development, meaning economic, social, and political development, and since “wisdom” becomes possible only at the end of that process, within the “ideal” communist society that brings it to completion, we can be even more precise.
The achievement of omniscience will crown the efforts made by humanity throughout its entire history.
So when philosophy attributes to humanity qualities normally attributed only to God, such as omniscience, the word “humanity” does not mean one isolated, exceptional, uniquely gifted person.
It means collective humanity: the whole human race taken together across the full course of its many historical forms and developments.
Marxist-Leninist-Stalinist philosophy—the philosophy of our time—can therefore aim consciously and openly at omniscience with pride, but without insane recklessness.
It knows, however, that “wisdom” can be achieved in practice only “in our time,” within the “ideal,” meaning final and communist, society—and that this society has not yet been fully realized.
It therefore knows that it is not yet, and cannot yet be, perfect knowledge.
It consciously aims at perfect knowledge, and it aims at it seriously, because it actively works to achieve it.
It knows that without conscious effort—without persistent work and decisive struggle—perfect knowledge will never be reached.
But while doing everything in its power to reach perfect knowledge, it also knows that it has not yet reached it.
In aiming at perfection, it recognizes its own imperfection.
And yet it assumes that its own imperfect knowledge is the only path by which perfect knowledge can be reached.
What, then, is this philosophical knowledge which is imperfect, knows itself to be imperfect, and nevertheless regards itself as the only route to perfect knowledge?

To answer this question, we must examine “true” philosophy from two different points of view: first as imperfect knowledge, and second as knowledge that knows its own imperfection and consciously aims at perfect knowledge.
On the one hand, if “wisdom” or perfect knowledge is omniscience, then imperfect philosophical knowledge is first of all partial or fragmentary knowledge.
But it is not partial in the way that, say, mathematical knowledge is partial, where the object of study is clearly limited and defined.
Partial philosophical knowledge is incomplete omniscience: it is one part of a whole that is ultimately meant to include everything.
On the other hand, philosophy knows that its knowledge is imperfect or incomplete.
This means that it asks questions which it ought in principle to be able to answer, but which it cannot yet in fact answer.
We can therefore say that philosophy is, in a certain sense, less the ability to answer questions than the art of asking them.
So when we speak about philosophy, we must first examine the problem of partial or fragmentary knowledge, and then clarify what this art of asking questions actually consists in.
That is what we must now do in this chapter, beginning with the problems raised by partial philosophical knowledge.
1. Philosophy as incomplete or imperfect knowledge, that is, as partial or fragmentary knowledge
There is no doubt that human beings possess what is usually called reason or intellect (ratio, logos). Because we have reason, we can produce articulated discourse (logos).

A discourse is called “articulated” when it can be broken down into distinct units, whether spoken or written. These units are called words. Words make up a discourse, but they can also be taken out of it and recombined in different ways to produce new discourses.
But if a discourse is to be intelligible—rational or logical—it must not only be articulated. Above all, it must be meaningful.

A discourse, and the words that make it up, have not only a sound or written form but also a semantic value. They must have a definite “meaning”: they must signify or refer to something. This semantic character is what makes articulated discourse understandable and communicable. A meaning understood by one person’s reason can, through meaningful discourse, be understood by the reason of another person. In this way, meaning can be passed from one person to another; one person can communicate it to another.

Now, there can hardly be meaning or communication without articulated expression, and there can be no rationality without communication. But these two features are still not enough to make a discourse rational in the strict sense.
A communicable discourse must also be coherent—that is, free of contradictions.

For a discourse to be coherent, anyone who understands it and makes its overall meaning their own must also be able to make sense of every word that forms part of it. Conversely, anyone who takes in the meaning of even one of its words must be able to relate that meaning to all the other words and to the overall meaning of the discourse they form together.
A discourse that fails this test is incoherent or contradictory. In that sense it is unintelligible, irrational, and false, even though it may still be meaningful, communicable, and articulated.
Every coherent discourse is therefore meaningful and articulated. But even this is not enough for complete rationality.
The discourse must also be convincing or demonstrable.
In other words, someone who hears and understands it must not merely be able to accept its meaning. They must also grasp that they are compelled to accept it.

Once a person has understood each of the words in the order in which they appear, they must necessarily accept the overall meaning of the discourse. And conversely, someone who accepts the overall meaning must necessarily accept the meanings of its component words and the order in which they occur.
A discourse of this kind is called true, and accepting it is called true knowledge.
A fully rational discourse is therefore one that is not only articulated, meaningful and communicable, and coherent or free of contradiction, but also true—that is, convincing or demonstrable.

When a rational human being encounters such a true discourse, they ultimately make it their own and are satisfied by it. Once they have understood it, they cannot simply discard it, replace it with another discourse, or even alter it in the slightest.

So when a rational—that is, speaking—human being produces or receives a true discourse, they stop producing further discourse. Their rational or logical activity comes to a halt. Instead of producing or searching for a new discourse, they simply repeat the true one.

A true discourse therefore brings the creative activity of reason—of discourse, of logos—to an end. And conversely, a discourse that finally brings this activity to an end is definitively, or absolutely, true.
The philosophical current known as rationalism assumes that human reason can reach “truth” entirely through its own resources—that is, through purely discursive or logical means.

According to rationalism, reaching truth does not require us to appeal to any “reality” that exists outside reason and independently of it, and which might “reveal” itself to human beings through non-discursive, or ir-ratio-nal, means such as sensory perception, desire, action, and so on.
Reason is supposed to be capable of satisfying us completely—that is, of finding “truth”—without ever leaving its own domain.

In other words, without going beyond the limits of meaningful and coherent discourse, human beings are supposed to be able to reach a discourse that brings their discursive activity to an end and can therefore be regarded as definitively, absolutely convincing, demonstrable, or true.
If we assume that this absolute and true discourse is complete discourse, then we can agree with the rationalist position.

As I have already said, complete discourse—or omniscience—fully satisfies reason and permanently brings its creative discursive activity to an end precisely because it contains every possible discourse.
Once such a discourse has been reached, reason has nothing new or different left to say. In the end, it can do nothing except repeat this complete discourse.
So we can indeed say that such a discourse is absolutely convincing to reason, that it satisfies reason fully and permanently, and that it can therefore be regarded as the truth.

Its completeness also determines its “circularity.” And this circular character can itself be established without stepping outside discourse. In this sense, rationalism is not mistaken when it claims that reason can itself establish the truth of the discourse it produces, independently of any extra-rational “reality” given in some non-rational experience.
All this is correct—but only if we regard complete discourse alone as truth.
In other words, it is valid only if we call omniscience, or perfect knowledge, genuine knowledge.
As soon as we are dealing with incomplete discourse and partial or fragmentary knowledge, the claims of rationalism break down.
And, as we will now see, rationalism itself became convinced of this during the course of its historical development.
Human beings can be said to have a “natural” tendency toward rationalism.
Until something convinces us otherwise, we tend to assume that any articulated, meaningful, and coherent discourse must also be convincing—that is, demonstrable or true.
A child, for example, is often very reluctant to answer a question with “I don’t know.” Usually the child says the first thing that comes to mind and is perfectly satisfied with the answer.
The same is true when children ask questions themselves. Almost any answer will satisfy them. As long as they understand what they are being told, they tend to assume that it is true.
Experience shows that this childlike credulity is hardly confined to children. It is found in most people, including people of very advanced age.

People say the most extraordinary nonsense. And they take this nonsense for truth simply because it has been stated to them in an articulated and meaningful way and—at best—without internal contradiction.

People are remarkably ready to “accept in good faith,” as an unquestionable truth, something they have in fact done no more than understand—especially when understanding it was difficult and took effort.
And how rarely does someone who has understood something then approach it “critically,” asking whether what they have understood is actually true.

This natural credulity—the almost irresistible tendency to regard every articulated and meaningful discourse as true without comparing it either with what actually exists or with what might be said differently about the same thing—completely characterizes the “childhood” of human history, the “primitive” period of rational or logical, that is, discursive activity.
This was the age in which myth-making flourished everywhere with extraordinary richness.
Only later did human beings begin to realize how much they did not know.

At first, even the most difficult questions were answered, so to speak, without hesitation. And however absurd those answers may have been, they were regarded as absolute truth not only by the people who gave them but also by the many people who heard them.
“First there was the Serpent, which laid the Egg, which gave birth to Earth and Heaven, which were then joined in sacred marriage,” and so on.

It is easy to see that the only reason for treating such a statement as true is the absence of contradiction, or the coherence, of the discourse that expresses it—and therefore the possibility of expressing it meaningfully and articulately.

In other words, during the age of myth-making, human beings assumed—unconsciously, of course, and therefore without saying so—that whenever reason produced an articulated discourse, it automatically and necessarily reached the truth.
The myth-maker can therefore be described as an extreme rationalist.

Any coherent discourse was taken as genuine knowledge. In practice, the myth-maker assumed that to know everything that could truly be known about objective reality, it was enough simply to obey the purely discursive or logical law of non-contradiction.
This extreme or radical rationalism can be called naive because the person who thought in this way had no awareness of the principle they were following.
Why should a discourse produced by reason necessarily “correspond” to a reality that exists independently of reason?
Naive rationalism not only failed to answer this question. It barely even asked it.
Why, then, did human beings abandon the position we are calling naive rationalism?
Why did they reject a viewpoint that initially seemed completely natural to them and that they had first accepted without qualification, even if unconsciously and without justification?

On the basis of psychological and historical experience, we can say with a high degree of confidence that they did not abandon it because their discourse repeatedly failed to match objective reality or experience.
